explanation: A revenue model explains what customers pay for and how receipts scale; a cost structure explains which resources are consumed as activity changes. Product sales, subscriptions, usage fees, advertising and transaction commissions create different margins and cash timing.

Revenue is not always gross customer spending: an intermediary may recognise only its fee under relevant principal-agent criteria. Analyse contribution, retention and capital needs alongside headline growth.

types.name: Advertising or commission
types.explanation: Monetise audience or facilitate another party's sale.

workedCase.setup: A marketplace processes ₹100 lakh customer orders and retains a 10% fee. Assume it is an agent and bears ₹6 operating costs.
steps: Recognised fee revenue under the assumption is ₹10.
Operating profit before other items is ₹10 − ₹6 = ₹4.
workedCase.result: Customer spending and the platform's revenue differ.
workedCase.interpretation: Contractual role, refunds and incentives determine actual recognition and economics.

analysis: Map payer, service and pricing unit.
Separate gross activity from retained revenue.
Classify cost drivers and funding needs.

explanation: Fixed costs remain unchanged within a relevant activity range; variable costs change with volume; semi-variable costs combine both. Some costs step upward when capacity thresholds are crossed. Classifying cost behaviour helps forecast contribution and break-even.
A cost is not permanently fixed or variable across all horizons. Rent can be fixed this year and adjustable later; labour may be partly flexible or constrained by minimum staffing.

types.name: Mixed or step cost
types.explanation: Combines a base with usage or capacity thresholds.

workedCase.setup: Monthly fixed cost is ₹100 and variable cost ₹2 per unit. Produce 50 units.
steps: At 100 units, total cost is ₹300 and cost per unit falls from ₹4 to ₹3.
workedCase.result: Higher utilisation spreads fixed cost without reducing variable cost per unit.
workedCase.interpretation: A capacity expansion could add a new fixed-cost step and change the comparison.

analysis: State the time horizon and range.
Model capacity steps and avoidable costs.

explanation: Contribution margin is revenue less costs that vary with the activity under the chosen definition. It first covers fixed costs; only the remainder is operating profit. Break-even volume equals fixed cost divided by unit contribution when prices and unit variable costs are constant.
Gross profit and contribution need not match because accounting cost-of-sales and managerial cost behaviour use different classifications. Multi-product break-even depends on sales mix.

types.name: Break-even point
types.explanation: Activity at which contribution equals fixed cost.

workedCase.setup: Price is ₹10 per unit, variable cost ₹6 and fixed cost ₹100.
workedCase.result: Sales below 25 units produce a loss under these assumptions.
workedCase.interpretation: Discounts, capacity steps or changing product mix require an updated model.

analysis: Test mix, price and capacity assumptions.

explanation: Price-volume-mix analysis separates revenue changes caused by price, quantity and product composition. The decomposition depends on the order and convention used; interaction terms must be handled consistently. It helps explain whether growth came from more units, better pricing or a richer mix.
Revenue effects do not translate one-for-one into profit. Products have different contribution and variable costs, and discounts can increase volume while reducing total margin.

types.name: Price effect
types.explanation: Changed selling price on a defined quantity base.

types.name: Volume effect
types.explanation: Changed units at a defined price base.

types.name: Mix effect
types.explanation: Changed proportions of products with different prices or margins.

workedCase.setup: One product sells 100 units at ₹10, then 120 at ₹11. Use base-price volume effect followed by price on current volume.
workedCase.result: A declared convention reconciles the full change.
workedCase.interpretation: With multiple products, isolate mix and consider contribution, not just revenue.

analysis: Translate revenue drivers into cost and profit effects.

explanation: Capacity utilisation measures output relative to usable capacity. Fixed-cost absorption can improve as utilisation rises, creating operating leverage. However, bottlenecks, overtime, maintenance and quality problems can make costs nonlinear near the limit.
Unused capacity can be intentional resilience or evidence of poor demand. The relevant denominator is practical usable capacity, not a theoretical maximum that ignores downtime.

workedCase.setup: Practical monthly capacity is 100 units and fixed costs ₹300. Output increases from 50 to 75 units.
steps: Fixed cost per unit falls from ₹6 to ₹4.
Assess whether variable costs or service quality change at the higher load.
workedCase.result: Spreading fixed costs improves unit economics within this range.
workedCase.interpretation: A new shift or machine can create another cost step; the relationship is not unlimited.

analysis: Separate fixed absorption from variable efficiency.
Test cost and quality near capacity limits.

explanation: Economies of scale reduce average cost as one activity expands; economies of scope reduce total cost from producing different activities together. Scale benefits can come from spreading fixed costs, purchasing or specialised processes. Scope benefits can come from shared distribution, data or infrastructure.
Greater size can also create diseconomies through coordination, complexity and weaker service. Claimed savings need an actual resource mechanism rather than a vague assertion that larger is better.

types.name: Scale economy
types.explanation: Lower unit cost with greater output.

types.name: Diseconomy
types.explanation: Complexity raises costs or reduces effectiveness.

workedCase.setup: Product A costs ₹100 lakh alone and B ₹80 alone. A shared delivery system makes combined cost ₹150.
steps: Check integration and shared-service costs before concluding the benefit persists.
workedCase.result: The saving arises from joint production, not merely more units of one product.
workedCase.interpretation: Savings can disappear if service requirements conflict or shared resources become bottlenecks.

analysis: Compare feasible standalone and combined costs.

explanation: Customer acquisition cost divides relevant acquisition spending by customers acquired under a stated cohort and attribution definition. Fully loaded CAC includes appropriate sales, marketing and onboarding resources; paid-channel CAC may include a narrower set. These measures should not be mixed.
Use genuinely acquired customers, not leads or downloads, and allow for sales-cycle lag. Low CAC is valuable only when retained contribution and customer quality justify the spending.

types.name: Fully loaded CAC
types.explanation: Includes specified staff and support resources.

workedCase.setup: Spend ₹1,200 acquiring 100 paying customers, while a further ₹300 sales-support cost is relevant.
steps: Compare each only with a lifetime-value measure of compatible scope.
workedCase.result: The definition changes the result materially.
workedCase.interpretation: Attribution, cohort timing and customers who would arrive organically affect causal interpretation.

analysis: Evaluate retained contribution rather than acquisition volume alone.

explanation: Customer lifetime value estimates the present value of future customer contribution under retention, spending, service-cost and discount assumptions. Revenue-based lifetime measures are not the same as contribution value. Acquisition cost should be subtracted or compared consistently.
A simple contribution/churn shortcut assumes stable behaviour and restrictive timing. Cohort models are preferable when customers expand, decline, reactivate or incur varying service costs.

types.name: Net customer value
types.explanation: LTV less acquisition and other included costs.

workedCase.setup: Assume a customer produces ₹100 annual contribution for three years, then leaves; discount rate is 10% and CAC ₹150.
steps: Stress shorter retention or lower contribution.
workedCase.result: Positive revenue alone would not establish positive net customer value.
workedCase.interpretation: The forecast must include actual service, payment and retention economics.

analysis: Use contribution rather than unqualified revenue.

explanation: Retention measures how much customer activity remains; churn measures loss under a specified definition. Customer-count retention differs from revenue retention because surviving customers can expand or contract. Cohort analysis follows customers acquired together to distinguish age effects from growth in new acquisitions.
Do not mix annual and monthly churn or infer long-run behaviour from a short early cohort. Net revenue retention can exceed 100% while some customers still leave.

types.name: Gross revenue retention
types.explanation: Existing revenue after losses and contraction, excluding expansion.

types.name: Net revenue retention
types.explanation: Includes expansion within the starting cohort.

workedCase.setup: A cohort begins with 100 customers paying ₹100 each. Ten leave; retained customers collectively add ₹2,000 spending.
steps: Assuming no contraction, gross revenue retention = ₹9,000/₹10,000 = 90%.
workedCase.result: Revenue can grow while customer count falls.
workedCase.interpretation: Expansion concentration and price increases should be separated from durable usage growth.

analysis: Compare cohorts rather than only total business growth.

explanation: Customer and product profitability allocates relevant revenue and costs to a defined unit. Direct contribution differs from profit after shared-cost allocation. A customer can buy high revenue while consuming costly returns, support or delivery.

Allocated overhead is not automatically avoidable. Decisions to discontinue should compare the cash consequences of removal, including stranded fixed costs, rather than relying only on an accounting allocation.

types.name: Fully allocated profit
types.explanation: Includes a stated share of common cost.

types.name: Avoidable profit effect
types.explanation: Costs and benefits changing if the unit is removed.

workedCase.setup: A customer generates ₹100 revenue, ₹70 direct cost and ₹35 allocated overhead. Assume only ₹10 of overhead is avoidable if the customer leaves.
steps: Dropping the customer loses ₹30 contribution but saves ₹10, reducing total profit by ₹20.
workedCase.result: An allocated loss does not automatically justify discontinuation.
workedCase.interpretation: Capacity constraints or better alternative customers can change the decision.

analysis: Distinguish direct, allocated and avoidable costs.
Compare actual alternatives and capacity use.

explanation: CAC payback estimates the time needed for customer contribution to recover acquisition spending. Use contribution after relevant ongoing costs rather than revenue. Discounted payback additionally reflects time value; both measures can ignore value after the recovery date.

Fast payback improves financing resilience but does not establish high lifetime value or long retention. A customer can repay CAC quickly and then leave, while a slower cohort may still create more total value.

workedCase.setup: CAC is ₹120 and monthly contribution ₹20, constant from the first month.
steps: At only ₹10 contribution, payback becomes 12 months.
If customers typically leave after four months, they do not recover the assumed CAC.
workedCase.result: Payback must fit observed retention and cost definitions.
workedCase.interpretation: Discounting and uneven onboarding costs require a dated cumulative schedule.

analysis: Assess liquidity and total customer value together.

explanation: Working-capital intensity measures operating-cycle funds tied up per unit of activity; capital intensity measures longer-lived resources needed for capacity. Growth in both can consume cash even when margins are stable. Asset-light businesses can still have substantial receivable or customer-acquisition funding needs.
Compare incremental needs, not only historical average ratios. New capacity may arrive in large steps and remain underutilised during ramp-up.

types.name: Incremental intensity
types.explanation: New capital needed for additional activity.

workedCase.setup: Revenue grows ₹100 lakh. Assume incremental operating working capital 20% of revenue and new equipment ₹30.
steps: Compare resulting cash contribution with this funding need.
workedCase.result: Growth can require ₹50 cash before all benefits arrive.
workedCase.interpretation: Supplier credit and customer advances may reduce the cycle requirement but add obligations.

analysis: Connect growth, capital utilisation and returns.

explanation: Network effects occur when participation improves value for other users, such as more buyers attracting sellers. They can support retention or pricing but also require incentives, moderation, reliability and sufficient local density. Network effects are not synonymous with economies of scale.
Financial analysis should show how participation changes contribution, acquisition cost or retention. A growing network subsidised indefinitely may fail to become economically self-supporting.

types.name: Same-side effect
types.explanation: Users benefit from more users on their side.

types.name: Negative effect
types.explanation: Congestion, poor quality or competition reduces user value.

workedCase.setup: A marketplace adds sellers and attracts buyers, but pays ₹20 lakh incentives to earn ₹12 extra contribution.
steps: Incremental current contribution net of incentive is −₹8.
Estimate whether later retention or density changes improve economics.
Test the required improvement rather than treating user growth as proof.
workedCase.result: A network mechanism needs a credible cash-economic bridge.
workedCase.interpretation: Benefits may be geographically limited or vulnerable to users joining several competing platforms.

explanation: Pricing changes contribution as well as demand. A discount reduces unit margin and must generate enough incremental volume or future benefit to compensate. Revenue management balances price, availability, capacity and customer willingness to pay under relevant constraints.

Price elasticity is context-dependent; historical promotions can be confounded by seasonality and selection. Test contribution after refunds, fulfilment and acquisition costs rather than simply observing higher sales.

types.name: List and realised price
types.explanation: Posted amount versus actual net receipt.

types.name: Discount strategy
types.explanation: Price reduction for a defined purpose.

types.name: Dynamic or segmented pricing
types.explanation: Prices vary with demand or customer context.

workedCase.setup: Price is ₹10 and variable cost ₹6, giving ₹4 contribution. A ₹1 discount reduces contribution to ₹3.
steps: To preserve total contribution, volume must rise by 4/3 − 1 ≈ 33.33%.
Check capacity and promotion costs before concluding the discount pays.
workedCase.result: A 10% price cut requires more than 10% extra volume here.
workedCase.interpretation: Customer retention and cannibalisation can alter the longer-term result.

analysis: Test demand, capacity and customer behaviour.

explanation: Driver-based analysis connects operational quantities with statements: customers × activity × price produces revenue; resources and unit costs produce expenses; timing and capacity produce working capital and assets. It makes forecasts inspectable rather than assuming every line grows with sales.
Drivers should be independent enough to avoid double counting. If both customer growth and total-volume growth represent the same expansion, multiplying them can inflate the forecast.

workedCase.setup: Assume 100 customers each buy 2 units at ₹10, with variable cost ₹6 per unit and fixed cost ₹300.
workedCase.result: Operational assumptions reconcile to financial results.
workedCase.interpretation: Collections, stock and capital spending need separate drivers to forecast cash.

analysis: Connect revenue and margin to cash and capital needs.

explanation: Unit economics connects a defined operating unit to revenue, variable costs, acquisition spending and the resources needed to serve it. The unit may be a product, customer, order, subscription or capacity slot. A positive gross margin does not establish positive contribution after delivery and acquisition costs, and an attractive mature customer can coexist with large early cash losses.

Cohorts help distinguish real improvement from changes in customer mix or survivorship. Lifetime value requires retention, margin, timing and discount assumptions; revenue alone is not customer value. Fixed costs and capital investment also matter when moving from a profitable unit to a profitable business.

types.name: Contribution
types.explanation: Revenue less the defined variable-cost perimeter.

types.name: Break-even
types.explanation: Activity required to cover relevant fixed costs.

types.name: Acquisition and retention
types.explanation: Costs and behaviour determining customer economics.

types.name: Capital intensity
types.explanation: Operating assets and cash required to sustain the model.

workedCase.setup: A product sells for ₹100 with ₹60 variable cost. Monthly fixed costs are ₹40,000; assume capacity is sufficient and no other costs.
steps: At 1,200 units, profit before other charges = 1,200 × ₹40 − ₹40,000 = ₹8,000.
workedCase.result: Positive unit contribution creates profit only after enough volume covers fixed costs.
workedCase.interpretation: A price discount changes contribution disproportionately, and growth may require new fixed capacity. Recheck the economics rather than assuming unlimited scale benefits.

analysis: Define the unit and cost perimeter.
Analyse cohorts, capacity and cash timing.
Connect unit contribution to whole-business investment and profit.
